title: Case study: Weekly Scorecard for a Performance Ad Agency
text:
## Case study: Weekly Scorecard for a Performance Ad Agency

Service: Operations & automation. Status: Parallel run · cutover Oct 2026. Kelvin's role: Ops & Automation Assistant · Penguin Ops · Sole builder: data, app and cutover.

A performance ad agency ran its weekly team targets from a Google Sheet that people typed into, and the script feeding it had quietly stopped recording results. I repaired the old system first, then replaced the sheet with a web app where every number is calculated from the source systems and nothing is typed.

Problem: The weekly scorecard decided what the team worked on, but its numbers were partly hand-entered and the Apps Script scanner behind it had stopped recording verdicts in early September. Nobody could say which numbers were current, and every correction relied on whoever typed last.
- Built: Repaired the V1 scanner and restored 130 lost verdicts, 119 of them dated from version history.
- Built: Fed a Postgres database from Asana webhooks on every client board, an hourly read of each campaign vault, and a daily Meta spend pull.
- Built: Wrote the metric engine as tested pure functions: rows in, numerator, denominator and value out.
- Built: Shipped the scorecard, an admin Control Panel with dated targets, a Data health page that explains anything that could make a number wrong or late, and a How it works guide for the team.
- Built: Added a Monday Slack digest of last week's hits and misses with reasons, and a sheet mirror so the familiar view stays.
- Built: Deployed on the agency's own Google Cloud (Cloud Run, Cloud Scheduler, Secret Manager) behind Google sign-in, with a parallel run and cutover plan.
- Outcome: 328 of 351 weekly values match the old sheet (93%), and all 23 differences trace to known V1 behaviour.
- Outcome: Derived events agree with V1 on all 12,785 events both systems hold.
- Outcome: 130 lost verdicts recovered before the switch.
- Stack: Next.js, Supabase (Postgres), Google Cloud Run, Cloud Scheduler, Asana API, Meta Marketing API, Google Apps Script, Slack

Service: Operations & automation. Status: In testing. Kelvin's role: Automation & Web Developer · Client engagement.

- Built: Wired the agents to run daily at 07:00 New York on real data only when they are switched on and their data is less than 45 days old, otherwise they wait instead of guessing.
- Built: Built a two-step purchase-order flow for low stock that opens a Monday.com task, email and SMS results pages and a UGC video agent, and started the Meta ads feed.

- Built: Generated structured HTML emails with full AI analysis, application reasoning, and a direct job link, turning a notification into an immediate action.

- What keeps it reliable: A duplicate client stops the run and alerts the team instead. If any step fails, the error workflow posts the client's name and the step that broke. Fee, ad account and start date land in ClickUp fields, so the reporting workflows can use them.
- 38 nodes; starts on Typeform: Onboarding General; uses Typeform, ClickUp, Slack.

title: n8n automation: Daily spend, ROAS and fee

## n8n automation: Daily spend, ROAS and fee

An n8n workflow Kelvin built, in the group "Client operations for a Google Ads agency". Built for: Penguin Ops, for a Google Ads agency.

title: n8n automation: Daily Shopify revenue
text:
## n8n automation: Daily Shopify revenue

An n8n workflow Kelvin built, in the group "Client operations for a Google Ads agency". Built for: Penguin Ops, for a Google Ads agency.
- Problem: Revenue lived in each client's own Shopify admin, so there was no daily figure per store to set against ad spend.
- What it does now: Every morning it pulls each connected store's orders, saves the day's total and Google-attributed revenue, and posts a summary to the ops channel.
- How it runs: Runs at 06:00 and re-pulls the last three days for every connected store, in the store's own timezone. Counts revenue as the order subtotal after discounts, before shipping. Marks an order as Google when the last visit before it came from Google. Saves orders and revenue per store per day, then posts the summary.
- What keeps it reliable: Test and cancelled orders are skipped. Re-pulling three days picks up late changes to recent orders. A store that fails is named in the summary while the others still save. A login-protected form backfills past days.

## n8n automation: Connect a Shopify store

text:
## n8n automation: AI support triage

An n8n workflow Kelvin built, in the group "AI agents and assistants".
- Problem: Every support email needed someone to read it, sort it and write a reply, and repeat emails got handled twice.
- What it does now: Each email is checked for duplicates, classified, saved and given a draft reply in Gmail. Only the ones that need a person get flagged.
- How it runs: A new email arrives in Gmail and is normalised. Airtable is checked for a duplicate, and the run stops if it's already there. The email is classified through an API and the result is validated before it's saved. A tone-aware reply is drafted and saved in Gmail. Anything that needs a person is flagged in Slack, and the alert is logged.
- What keeps it reliable: Duplicates stop before any work is done. The classification is validated before anything relies on it. Each record moves through clear statuses in Airtable: processing, draft ready or needs review. Replies stay as drafts. Nothing is sent automatically.

text:
## n8n automation: Lead diagnostic intake

An n8n workflow Kelvin built, in the group "Pipelines, intake and alerts". Built for: Stakra. It is running in production.
- Problem: People who stopped halfway through the diagnostic were lost, and the ones who finished waited for someone to put their results together.
- What it does now: Partial and complete responses are both saved to Notion, and every completed diagnostic gets a results email built from Notion content.

The lead is marked as sent, or as failed if the email didn't go.

An n8n workflow Kelvin built, in the group "Pipelines, intake and alerts". It is running in production.

- What it does now: React with ❌ to a bot message and it's deleted, along with the thread it started.
- How it runs: Slack reports a new reaction. Checks that it's a ❌ on a bot message. Fetches the thread if the message started one. Deletes the message, or every message in the thread.
- What keeps it reliable: Any other reaction is ignored. It can only delete the bot's own messages.
